worksheet.title: Does the Order Work?
worksheet.subtitle: Read the algorithm and check the order
worksheet.learning_goal: I can tell if an algorithm's steps are in an order that works.

parts.title: Check the order
parts.text: Read each algorithm. Does the order make sense? Circle YES if it works, or NO if a step is in the wrong place. Then tell why. A step that needs another step must come AFTER it.

parts.title: Does A work?
parts.prompt: Circle YES or NO. Tell why the order does or does not work.

blocks.label: 3. pour the cereal in the bowl

parts.title: Does B work?
parts.prompt: Circle YES or NO. Tell what is wrong with the order.

parts.title: Algorithm C — go down the slide
You try — C does not work
parts.prompt: Circle YES or NO. Then write the 3 steps of C in an order that DOES work.

parts.title: Big idea
parts.text: An algorithm only works if every step comes after the steps it needs. If a step is in the wrong place, the order does not work — even if all the steps are there.

teacher_guide.title: Does the Order Work?
teacher_guide.subtitle: Quick facilitation notes & answer key
teacher_guide.footer_topic: 5. Does the Order Work? — Teacher Guide

parts.title: Goal
parts.text: Students read three algorithms and judge whether the order works, explaining why, then rewrite a broken one so it works. Reading existing code and describing how its order affects whether it succeeds is C3.2; rewriting the broken order into a working one is C3.1.

parts.title: Ontario curriculum (Grade 1 — C3 Coding)
text: C3.1 — solve problems and create computational representations of mathematical situations by writing and executing code, including code that involves sequential events.
C3.2 — read and alter existing code, including code that involves sequential events, and describe how changes to the code affect the outcomes.

parts.title: Materials
parts.text: The printed worksheet and a pencil. Optional: act out each algorithm so a wrong order is obvious (you can't slide before you sit at the top).

parts.title: Run it (about 20 min)
text: 1. I DO: read Algorithm A. 'You need the circle before you can add rays — so this order works.'
2. WE DO: Exercise 1 — A works (YES). Exercise 2 — B does NOT work; you can't eat before pouring the cereal and milk.
3. YOU DO: Exercise 3 — C does NOT work; rewrite it: climb the ladder, sit at the top, slide down.
4. Connect: 'All the right steps still fail if they are in the wrong order — order is part of the code.'

parts.title: Answer key (modelled by the run-gate)
text: Ex 1 — A WORKS (YES): you draw the circle first, then add rays and colour it; each step has what it needs.
Ex 2 — B does NOT work (NO): eating is first, but you must pour the cereal then the milk before you can eat. Eating should be last.
Ex 3 — C does NOT work (NO). A working order: climb the ladder, sit at the top, slide down (you must sit at the top before you can slide down).

parts.title: Watch for & differentiate
text: Common slip: saying an order works because all the steps are present — point out that the POSITION of a step matters, not just that it is there.
Simplify: act out Algorithm C; the wrong order becomes obvious when you try to slide before sitting.
Extend: ask students to break Algorithm A on purpose by moving one step, and explain why it no longer works.
Success indicator: the child marks A=YES, B=NO, C=NO and rewrites C as climb, sit, slide with a reason.
